1:
The first question is who is addressed, and Calvin stands nearly alone. He takes the northern kingdom, and meets the obvious objection himself: those ten tribes had been carried off and the kingdom had ended years before. His answer is that the oracle is partly prophecy and partly doctrine, so the exiles might learn why they were driven out, since punishment is useless until God convinces men of its cause; and further, that many were still there, because the Assyrian could not have transported so many thousands without burdening his own kingdom, and so took the flower of the people and left the commonalty behind. Those who remained went on in their abominations, unmoved by their brothers exile or their own losses, which is why another judgment had to be pronounced. Gill, Clarke and Henry all take the other side. Gill says the ten tribes had gone long since and reads Judea, though he allows that the prophecy may show the reason for the older captivity or address those of the ten still mixed among the other tribes. Clarke is blunt that Israel simply means Judea. Henry takes it for the whole land.

The dating is given three ways. Gill reports from Junius that it came on a sabbath in the sixth year of the captivity of Jehoiachin, more than a year after the vision at Chebar. Clarke places it after the four hundred and thirty days of lying on his side were done. Calvin fixes it from the opening of the book, concluding that the prophet spoke after the ten tribes were dispersed.

Keil and Delitzsch supply the plan. Two further oracles develop the earlier signs into the extent of the judgment: desolation to the idolatrous places and through them to the land, destruction to the idolaters, then a remnant scattered among the heathen who come to be converted, and last a repeated account of the necessity and terrible character of what is coming.

Why the mountains are addressed rather than the men draws a rare unanimity. Ellicott notes that prophetic utterances are often addressed to inanimate objects as a poetic way of representing the people, and that the mountains are named as the chosen places of idolatrous worship, the sun-god Baal being worshipped on the hills. Clarke gives the same reason briefly. Wesley reads them as the inhabitants of the mountains, secure in their fastnesses. Gill and Calvin both hear an insult in the address. Gill says it was as well or better to speak to the mountains than to the Jews, who had so often put the word away that they were unworthy of it, so the direction carries a degree of indignation. Calvin says God obliquely signifies they were deaf and unworthy of the labour spent on them, and recalls the prophet sent against Jeroboam who turned from the king to address the altar. Henry makes the mountains a shame to men who would not listen, and pictures the prophet setting his face as a judge looks at a prisoner, these having been holy mountains until the high places polluted them.

Henry alone follows the threat through. God is commander-in-chief of the expedition, and the sword of the Chaldeans goes where he sends it and lights where he directs it. From that he draws four observations: that war makes desolations which not even the most sacred persons and places escape; that God sometimes ruins idolatries by the hands of idolaters, the Chaldeans being great admirers of their own gods and great despisers of everyone else; that it is just with God to make a desolation of what we make an idol of, since he will not bear a rival; and that if men will not destroy idolatry he will find a way, the high places Josiah pulled down having been set up again, and now to fall to the sword of war.
3:
The word rendered rivers is disputed. Ellicott would render it ravines, deep valleys along which a stream might sometimes run, and notes that such places were favourites for idolatrous rites, especially the worship of the Phoenician Astaroth, paired with Baal. Calvin reports that Jerome translated it rocks, observes that the word is used of whatever is violent, and is content with rocks or torrents. Wesley reads through to the inhabitants, those who dwell by rivers or in the valleys. Calvin explains why both heights and hollows are named: on the mountains they thought themselves near to God, while in the valleys they performed their rites in shade and obscurity, imagining themselves hidden as in a sanctuary.

Calvin presses the figure until it breaks. A sword cannot injure a mountain, since one stone would break a thousand swords and remain entire; so the sword stands for death, and the address to the mountains is an oblique address to men, whose deafness made God turn from them to speak to mute things. Ellicott catches a different emphasis, on the doubled pronoun: because these judgments were to be worked out by human hands, attention might settle on secondary causes, and by claiming them beforehand God makes it evident that all was from him.

The images divide the voices again. Clarke says they are literally sun images. Ellicott agrees and adds that the verse is drawn from the law, where the same woes were foretold by Moses if the people disobeyed, which has now come to pass. Calvin knows the derivation from a root meaning heat and grants that some take it of the sun, but calls that divination too contracted, preferring to name the idols from the mad love with which their worshippers were seized, since the prophets compare idolaters to adulterers running after harlots. Of the other word for idols he notes that it comes from foulness, even filth, and draws from this that men who thrust in their own fictions provoke wrath rather than render worship.

The corpses laid before the idols are read as poetic justice. Ellicott points out that nothing was so defiling under the law as the touch of a dead body, so a people who defiled the land with idols will have the idols defiled by their dead, worshipped no longer by the living but by prostrate bodies. Calvin makes it a legible sign: mixing bones with the victims was detestable in every sacrifice, so anyone not blind could read from it that the whole worship had been abominable. Clarke reports the literal fulfilment by the Chaldeans, citing the account in Baruch that they opened the sepulchres of the chief people and threw the bones about. Wesley notes that the idols were upbraided with their inability to help.

Ellicott notes the strength of the word rendered abolished, and finds an irony in it: this is what Israel should have done to the nations of Canaan, and having failed of that command their own works, done in imitation of those they supplanted, must be blotted out instead. Calvin builds a rule of worship on the same word. By works the prophet means not idols of wood or metal but whatever men have fashioned and ascribe to themselves rather than take from the mouth of God; obtrude nothing of our own and worship is pure, add anything and it is an abomination. On the last verse Gill notes that the word for slain is singular and may stand for the plural, as the Septuagint takes it, unless a principal person is meant, though Zedekiah was not slain. Ellicott asks whether the mountains are still addressed and decides the figure has been gradually dropped. Calvin adds why the formula of knowing is needed: the Israelites did not openly deny God, but had no faith in the prophet words, so an avenger is set behind the teaching they despised.
8:
Henry marks the turn: mercy rejoices here against judgment, a sad end being made of the people but not a full end. He calls it a little remnant, a few of many, left only because God leaves them, since they deserved to be cut off with the rest. Gill locates it not in Judea but in Babylon and the countries of dispersion. Calvin gives the promise a hard edge. God does not offer simple pardon, leaving them safe in their own land, but says their safety shall be in exile; the life promised is a wretched one, obtained only through a kind of death. Wesley says it is the Lord who preserves them. Ellicott looks past the immediate case, calling this the divine plan set out by Paul, of purifying the people by setting aside the mass and showing mercy to a remnant, which looks far beyond this captivity, as the prophecy of Zechariah shows, uttered after the return. Then the cloud settles down again.

Henry reads the remnant as both preserved and penitent. They are reprieved to have time to return, since to those whom God designs for life he gives repentance unto life; his patience leaves room for repentance and encourages it, though many who have the space want the grace. The occasion is a mixture of judgment and mercy, driven out of their land but not out of the living. The root is memory: those who forgot God in prosperity remember him in captivity, as the prodigal never thought of home until ready to perish in the far country. Sin takes its rise in forgetting God, and repentance in remembering him. Clarke reports it as history: those who escaped saw whose hand it was and have worshipped God alone ever since. Gill notes two readings of what is remembered, the grace of God after Jarchi or the fear of him after the Targum.

The clause about being broken is the crux, and three answers are given. Ellicott observes that the verb is passive in form but is better taken, with most modern commentators, as a middle in a transitive sense, so that God has broken their whorish heart and their eyes, the eyes being the means by which the heart was drawn to evil. Wesley reads it as grief. Calvin sets out a double sense and chooses. It may mean that God was at last conquered by their wickedness, having found no profit in bearing them; or it may be referred to pardon, since a man who willingly forgives injuries is said to be broken. He judges the first more suitable.

Calvin then makes repentance itself the scarce thing. Chastisement is common to the elect and the reprobate, and many are made worse by it, first roaring, then outrageous, then rushing into a madness in which they would wage war with God if they could reach so far. Since no difference can be found between the few spared and the multitude that perished except that it pleased God to keep a seed, their repentance is a singular gift. The exile itself was useful, since as long as they held the holy land they provoked him as if on purpose.

The self-loathing that follows is the mark of the real thing. Ellicott says it indicates true repentance, since they loathe the sin and themselves for having committed it, and traces the chain: sin drew punishment, punishment destroyed many but brought a remnant to repentance, which leads to a knowledge of God. Wesley finds three ingredients in it: grief towards God, indignation against themselves, abhorrence of the offence. Henry presses the marriage figure they all use, since idolatry is spiritual whoredom and the breach of a covenant; and he notices the order, that their hearts followed their eyes in choosing gods, since they must have gods they could see, and then their eyes followed their hearts in adoring them.
10:
Calvin makes the knowing here the fruit of repentance rather than a further threat. The people had trifled while the prophets threatened, and because they listened only to men they supposed they were contending with Jeremiah or Ezekiel alone, with impunity against mere mortals. God answers that he was the chief author of what they despised. When they repent they will perceive he did not speak in vain; from which Calvin draws a lesson for his own hearers, to tremble in time and treat any sign of indignation as though execution were at hand. Wesley notes that in vain means either without cause, their sins having given just cause, or without effect.

The gesture draws the widest range of comment in the chapter, and two voices are arguing with different opponents. Gill describes it as the behaviour of people in distress, striking one hand against the other, and follows the Hebrew in making the second action an extension of the foot, or with the Syriac a beating of the earth. Keil and Delitzsch call clapping and stamping gestures of violent excitement. Ellicott agrees that they mark strong emotion, showing an unchangeable determination joined to a sense of grievous wrong. Calvin explains why a sign is added: words moved them little, and God follows his custom in obstinate cases, so the gesture is for their sake, since when God thunders they remain secure and do nothing but laugh. Henry defends the gestures against those who call them antic and ridiculous, answering that God commanded them because they might drive the word home, so that a man who knows the worth of souls will be content to be laughed at by the wits if he may edify the weak. Clarke turns the other way and attacks those who argue from this verse for clapping and stamping in public worship: consistency would require copying his other typical actions too, lying on one side for three hundred and ninety days and the other for forty, shaving the head and burning the hair; what was proper in a prophet because commanded would in them be evidence of insanity.

Henry finds two things lamented in the cry: national sin, since the sins of sinners are the sorrows of the faithful servants of God, and national judgment, over which it is a duty to be affected not only by our own sufferings but by other people, as Christ beheld Jerusalem and wept over it.

The three punishments are then distributed, and every voice makes the same point, that the distribution offers no escape. Henry sets out three false securities: the man far off thinks himself beyond the arrows of the Chaldeans and is not beyond the arrows of God; the man near a place of strength falls by the sword before he can retreat; the man cautious enough to stay in the city dies of famine, the saddest death of all. Gill puts it flatly, that there is no fleeing from God, who has various ways to execute his wrath. Ellicott warns against over-reading the arrangement: all the forms of punishment fall upon the whole people, and we are not to think one kind reserved for one class and another for another, since those who escape one will fall by another. Calvin asks why these three are always named. It is not that God punishes only so, since he has innumerable hidden methods, but that this scourge is the most familiar; and he unfolds what each carries, since once men take up arms the gate is opened to robbery, burning and all violence, while in pestilence the husband deserts the wife. Henry closes on the bodies laid among the idols: they lived among them and shall die among them, and where they had offered sweet odours their carcases will send out an offensive smell, as if to atone for that misplaced incense.
13:
Calvin distinguishes the knowledge announced here from the one promised to the remnant. There the survivors were to remember and be ashamed; here only the experimental knowledge common to the ungodly, which frightens without bending anyone to humility. He takes the phrase widely, of all the Israelites even those who perish, the proof of vengeance being so conspicuous that they were compelled to feel their punishment just. What makes the vengeance unmistakable, he adds, is that it falls where the idols stand, the worshippers dropping beside the gods under whose protection they thought themselves safe.

Ellicott notes that the places are listed one after another to give the judgment vividness, and catches an irony: the phrase sweet savour belongs to the sacrifices God commanded, and is used here of the idol sacrifices. Calvin presses it into a figure, that God complains of being provoked by that foul incense as a husband is angered when an immodest woman sets herself to please an adulterer. He adds that no place is left uncondemned, since when the worshippers had their fill of high places they went down to shady valleys and set their altars under trees.

Calvin explains the stretching out of the hand as a concession to human dullness. God accomplishes everything by his nod, but since we do not grasp his judgment, Scripture pictures him extending the arm as men do for something great. Gill marks the preposition: the hand is stretched not to them in mercy but upon them in judgment, as the Targum also has it. Of the pair of words for the ruin Calvin prefers desolation and waste to a desolation and an astonishment.

The wilderness named at the end is the hardest point in the chapter, and the voices divide on its identity and location. Ellicott observes that the singular name occurs nowhere else, while the dual form is known as a double city on the eastern border of Moab, beyond which the great desert stretches nearly to the Euphrates; and since a wilderness took the name of the nearest town, this one seems proverbial for desolation. Wesley agrees on Moab, where the fiery serpents troubled Israel, and adds that Canaan is in his own day among the most desolate countries. Clarke gives the same location, part of that horrible wilderness of serpents and drought, but says the reason for naming it is not evident, and reports a conjecture that the place is really Riblah, where the princes of Israel were killed and Zedekiah blinded. The difference lies between two letters often scarcely distinguishable in manuscripts, which accounts for vast numbers of variant readings; five or six copies collated by Kennicott read it the second way, as do two of his own oldest, but all the ancient versions keep the first; and he insists pains should be taken to recover even one lost letter of the word of God.

Calvin knows the same variant, allows an error may have crept in from the similarity of the letters, and decides no change is needed. His sharper quarrel is with the syntax. He rejects as absurd the rendering that runs from the desert as far as this place, since the threat is against Israel while Diblath lay beyond it in Syria, thought by some to be Antioch; the particle marks a comparison, and Israel is to be made worse than that desert. What he likes about the comparison is that the exiles had already walked through that desert. Syria is fertile and Antioch, as geographers report, has an excellent site, so men who had crossed an opulent country and come out into a waste vast and sorrowful would be woken by the contrast. He closes on the naming: the prophet drops out and God comes forward as if speaking himself, because the calling was so plainly marked that no one could contend with the man without opposing God.
